one_sentence: The divine-human relationship described in Scripture shares the same 2D anxiety-avoidance topology as attachment theory, with worship postures mapping to attachment styles.
executive_summary: This document establishes a structural isomorphism between attachment theory in developmental psychology and the theology of prayer and worship. It maps four attachment styles (secure, anxious-preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, fearful-avoidant) onto four worship postures (secure trust, anxious legalism, avoidant deism, disorganized trauma-theology) using a shared 2D space of anxiety and avoidance. Key structural correspondences include secure base as divine refuge, proximity seeking as prayer, separation protest as lament, internal working models as theology proper, and earned security as sanctification. The mapping yields testable predictions: attachment anxiety predicts legalistic theology, attachment avoidance predicts deism, and spiritual abuse produces disorganized attachment to God. The isomorphism is empirically supported by the Attachment to God Inventory and has bidirectional implications for pastoral care and psychological theory.
short_summary: This document is a structural isomorphism record mapping attachment theory to Christian theology of prayer and worship. The core claim is that worship postures distribute across the same 2D anxiety-avoidance space as attachment styles, with four quadrants corresponding to secure, anxious, avoidant, and disorganized patterns. Key evidence includes ten structural correspondences (secure base, proximity seeking, separation protest, internal working model, earned security, attachment hierarchy) and empirical support from the Attachment to God Inventory. This matters because it provides a testable framework for understanding how relational history shapes theology and worship, with implications for pastoral care and spiritual formation.
